methods.label: Follow the forced neighbors
methods.explanation:
Write \(R_k\) for the red card numbered \(k\) and \(B_k\) for the blue card numbered \(k\). With five red cards and four blue cards alternating, both ends must be red. Every card away from the ends has two neighbors.

The only blue card divisible by \(4\) is \(B_4\), so \(R_4\) cannot have two blue neighbors and must be an end card. Similarly, \(R_5\) must be at the other end, next to \(B_5\). Reversing a stack does not change its middle-three sum, so start from the \(R_5\) end.

The next card is \(B_5\). Its other red neighbor must be \(R_1\), because the only red numbers dividing \(5\) are \(1\) and \(5\). Now \(B_3\) must have \(R_1\) and \(R_3\) as its two neighbors, since those are its only red divisors. This forces the beginning
\[
R_5,\ B_5,\ R_1,\ B_3,\ R_3.
\]
The other blue neighbor of \(R_3\) must be \(B_6\). The other red neighbor of \(B_6\) must then be \(R_2\), since \(R_1\) and \(R_3\) are already used. The remaining cards are \(B_4\) and \(R_4\), giving
\[
R_5,\ B_5,\ R_1,\ B_3,\ R_3,\ B_6,\ R_2,\ B_4,\ R_4.
\]
This order satisfies every divisibility condition. Every step was forced after choosing an orientation, so its reversal is the only other possibility. The middle three cards, in positions \(4,5,6\), have numbers \(3,3,6\). Their sum is \(\boxed{12}\), choice E.
